description: 30+ end-to-end problems: Parking Lot, Elevator, Movie Booking, Splitwise, Vending Machine, Cache, Rate Limiter.

topics.title: Parking Lot System (Beginner)
topics.definition: A multi-level parking lot system managing distinct vehicle types, parking spot allocation strategies, multi-floor navigation, real-time availability tracking, and automated ticket/fee calculation.
topics.why_it_matters: The classic canonical LLD interview problem. Tests your mastery of inheritance hierarchies (Vehicle vs Spot), Strategy pattern for spot assignment, State pattern for spot status, and thread-safe concurrent entry/exit.
topics.real_world_analogy: Think of an automated airport parking garage: an automated gate scans vehicle dimensions, assigns the nearest available compact/handicapped/large bay via an electronic sign, issues a ticket with a cryptographic hash timestamp, and bills you upon exit.
conceptual_breakdown: Core Entities: Vehicle (Motorcycle, Car, Bus), ParkingSpot (Small, Medium, Large, Handicapped), ParkingFloor, ParkingLot (Singleton/Facade).
Allocation Strategy: IParkingStrategy with concrete strategies like NearestToEntranceStrategy or BestFitStrategy.
Ticket & Billing: Ticket stores entry time, spot pointer, license plate. FeeCalculator strategy calculates hourly/flat pricing.
Concurrency Considerations: Atomic or mutex-guarded spot reservation to prevent double-booking across simultaneous entrance gates.

interactive_animation.title: Vehicle Entry, Spot Assignment & Exit Flow

steps.description: Vehicle (SUV/Car) arrives at Entry Gate 1.
ParkingLot queries IParkingStrategy to find optimal available Spot.
Spot #F1-S12 is atomically marked as OCCUPIED and linked to vehicle.
Ticket is generated with UUID, timestamp, and returned to driver.
Vehicle exits at Exit Gate: Ticket scanned, duration computed, Fee calculated, Spot liberated.

step_by_step_explanation: 1. Vehicle Type Hierarchy: Base class Vehicle with Motorcycle, Car, and Bus subclasses, using VehicleType enum for quick matching.
2. ParkingSpot Fitting Logic: canFitVehicle encapsulates the domain rule that Small fits only bikes, Medium fits cars/bikes, Large fits all.
3. Granular Spot-level Mutex: ParkingSpot has its own std::mutex to allow multiple entrance gates to assign distinct spots concurrently without contention.
4. Strategy Pattern for Billing: IFeeCalculator decouples variable pricing rules (peak vs off-peak vs flat hourly) from parking orchestration.
5. Ticket Lifecycle: Parking ticket stores timestamped snapshot data, preventing mutable reference leaks.

comparison_matrix.title: Spot Allocation Architectures
rows: Natural if heap keyed by distance

common_mistakes.mistake: Using a single global lock for all floors and spots
common_mistakes.correction: Use fine-grained per-spot locks or concurrent ring queues to ensure multiple entrance gates process cars simultaneously.

common_mistakes.mistake: Hardcoding ticket billing directly inside ParkingLot class
common_mistakes.correction: Use the Strategy Pattern (`IFeeCalculator`) so pricing rules can vary by day/time/discounts without editing core parking lot logic.
ParkingSpot aggregates Vehicle (spot owns reference to parked vehicle, not the other way around).

interview_traps:
Trap: 'How do you handle multiple entry and exit gates running on 8 different threads simultaneously?'
Answer: Discuss lock granularity: instead of locking the entire ParkingLot, maintain thread-safe concurrent priority queues (Min-Heaps by distance) per spot type with condition variables, or reader-writer locks per floor.

Trap: 'How would you handle oversized vehicles like EV charging spots or buses requiring 3 consecutive regular spots?'
Answer: Introduce a Composite spot model or an explicit MultiSpotReservation transaction that locks all required spots atomically.

code_refactor_exercise.problem: Refactor a monolithic God-class parking lot where ticket pricing, spot searching, and vehicle validation are all tightly coupled inside one 500-line function.

practice_problem.title: Design Dynamic Pricing & EV Spot Support
practice_problem.description: Extend the parking lot implementation to support EV charging spots with kilowatthour meter billing in addition to hourly parking fees.
practice_problem.hint: Use the Decorator pattern or a specialized EVFeeCalculator combining base parking duration with power meter telemetry.

topics.title: Elevator System (Beginner)
topics.definition: A multi-elevator dispatching and controller system managing hall calls (external floor buttons), car calls (internal floor buttons), direction scheduling (SCAN / LOOK algorithm), and door safety interlocks.
topics.why_it_matters: A quintessential test of State Pattern (Idle, Moving Up, Moving Down, Maintenance), Strategy Pattern (LOOK vs Shortest Seek Time vs Sector dispatching), and asynchronous Producer-Consumer task processing.
topics.real_world_analogy: Modern skyscraper elevators where a central dispatcher algorithm groups passengers going to the same skylobby zone into Elevator B, minimizing total transit time and stops.
conceptual_breakdown: ElevatorCar: Encapsulates current floor, direction, state (Idle, MovingUp, MovingDown), and pending destination requests (bitset or priority queues).
ElevatorController: Manages movement loop, door open/close timers, and floor step processing.
Dispatcher / Scheduler: IElevatorStrategy chooses which elevator handles external HallCalls (e.g. Look Algorithm, SCAN).
Direction & State: State pattern to strictly control valid state transitions (cannot open door while Moving).

steps.description: Elevator at Floor 1 (IDLE). Hall calls arrive: Floor 5 (UP), Floor 3 (DOWN), Floor 7 (UP).
Elevator starts Moving UP. Passes Floor 3 (ignored because direction is UP).
Elevator stops at Floor 5, opens door, passenger presses internal Floor 8.
Elevator serves Floor 7, then Floor 8 (highest requested floor).
No higher UP requests. Elevator reverses to Moving DOWN and serves Floor 3.

step_by_step_explanation: 1. LOOK Algorithm Data Structures: Using std::set (ascending) for UP floors and std::set> (descending) for DOWN floors guarantees $O(\log N)$ insertion and constant smallest-floor extraction.
2. State Encapsulation: Direction and movement state ensure elevator never violates physics (reversing direction midway without servicing higher requested floors).
3. Proximity Scoring Dispatcher: Dispatcher calculates weighted Manhattan distance favoring elevators moving towards the caller in the desired direction.
4. Tick-based Step Engine: step() advances elevator simulation state cleanly without blocking the dispatching thread.

common_mistakes.mistake: Handling elevator movement with blocking `sleep()` inside request handlers
common_mistakes.correction: Use asynchronous worker loops or tick-based state updates so client requests remain non-blocking.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using a single queue for requests causing erratic up-and-down oscillation
common_mistakes.correction: Implement LOOK algorithm with separate Up and Down ordered sets.

interview_traps:
Trap: 'How do you prevent starvation if floors 1 and 2 keep generating requests while someone at floor 50 is waiting?'
Answer: SCAN/LOOK guarantees bounded latency because the elevator must reach its extreme requested floor before reversing direction, preventing upper floor starvation.

code_refactor_exercise.problem: Refactor a monolithic switch-statement elevator where state checks (door open, moving, idle) are mixed with I/O and motor commands.
code_refactor_exercise.good_code: Use the State Pattern: IDLEState, MovingState, DoorOpenState classes implementing IElevatorState with explicit transitions.

practice_problem.title: Design VIP Elevator & Fire Emergency Mode
practice_problem.description: Add support for an emergency fire alarm signal that forces all elevator cabs to instantly abandon pending queues and descend directly to Ground Floor (Floor 1).
practice_problem.hint: Use Observer pattern to broadcast EmergencyEvent and clear both `upRequests` and `downRequests`.

topics.title: Vending Machine System (Beginner)
topics.definition: A state-driven automated snack and beverage dispenser managing inventory, currency acceptance, exact change calculation, product dispensing, and transaction rollbacks.
topics.why_it_matters: The gold standard interview question for testing the **State Pattern**. Cleanly decouples machine states (Idle, ReadyForSelection, Dispensing, Refunding) from business actions.
topics.real_world_analogy: A smart beverage vending machine: you insert a $5 bill (transitions to HasMoneyState), select B3 cold brew (DispensingState), coil motor turns, optical sensor verifies drop, and change returned (IdleState).
conceptual_breakdown: State Pattern Hierarchy: IVendingMachineState interface with IdleState, HasMoneyState, DispensingState, OutOfOrderState.
Inventory Management: Inventory managing items with aisle codes (e.g. 'A1', 'B2'), quantity, and price.
Coin / Cash Box: Manages coin denominations for change calculation using greedy or DP coin-change algorithm.
Transaction Isolation: Cancellation at any state refunds the exact deposited amount safely.

steps.description: Machine in IdleState. User inserts $2.00 bill.
Machine transitions to HasMoneyState (Balance: $2.00).
User selects 'A1' (Soda: $1.50). Machine validates stock & balance.
Transitions to DispensingState: Drops soda, decrements stock.
Calculates change ($0.50), returns coin, and transitions back to IdleState.

step_by_step_explanation: 1. State Pattern Decoupling: Each machine state (Idle, HasMoney, Dispensing) is an isolated object implementing IVendingMachineState.
2. Eliminating Fragile Conditionals: Avoided hundreds of nested if (state == 1) ... else if (state == 2) branches.
3. Transaction Safety: Refund logic in HasMoneyState cleanly returns money and resets balance without side effects.
4. Physical Hardware Isolation: Dispensing state cannot be aborted midway, protecting mechanical motor state.

comparison_matrix.title: State Pattern vs Enum Switch Design
rows: All logic for a state resides in one file
Easy to forget break; or invalid transition

common_mistakes.correction: DispensingState rejects `insertMoney` calls to prevent money swallowing.

common_mistakes.mistake: Deducting inventory before validating payment sufficiency
common_mistakes.correction: Validate balance >= item.price before decrementing stock.

interview_traps:
Trap: 'What if the mechanical dispenser jams and the sensor reports no item dropped?'
Answer: Discuss the Compensation / Rollback transaction: the state machine catches HardwareJamException, does NOT decrement inventory, refunds the customer's balance, and transitions to OutOfOrderState.

code_refactor_exercise.problem: Refactor a vending machine implemented with an int state variable and 10 nested if-statements.
code_refactor_exercise.good_code: Encapsulate each state in a class implementing IVendingMachineState.

practice_problem.title: Design Denomination-Limited Change Return
practice_problem.description: Implement a Greedy/DP Coin Dispenser that returns change using available $1, $0.25, $0.10, and $0.05 coins or warns the user if exact change is unavailable.
practice_problem.hint: Maintain an internal `unordered_map<CoinType, int>` cash inventory inside CashBox.

topics.title: Splitwise / Expense Sharing App (Intermediate)
topics.definition: A collaborative expense-sharing and balance settlement engine supporting multiple split strategies (Equal, Exact, Percentage, Shares) and graph-based debt simplification.
topics.why_it_matters: Tests your ability to design flexible Strategy Patterns for complex financial calculations and solve graph debt minimization (Min-Cash-Flow algorithm).
topics.real_world_analogy: Group travel with friends where Alice pays for the $120 dinner, Bob pays $60 for gas, and Charlie pays $30 for snacks. The app calculates who owes whom and minimizes total bank transfers.
conceptual_breakdown: User & Group Entities: User (id, name), Group (members, expenses).
Expense & Split Strategy: Expense contains payer, amount, and a list of Split objects computed via ISplitStrategy (Equal, Exact, Percentage).
Balance Sheet: Directed debt graph represented as unordered_map>.
Debt Simplification Algorithm: Greedy balance matching to reduce $N$ pairwise debts down to at most $N-1$ settlement transactions.

classes.name: ExpenseManager
methods: + addExpense(paidBy: string, amount: double, splits: vector<Split>, strategy: unique_ptr<ISplitStrategy>): void

steps.description: Initial Debts: Alice owes Bob $40. Bob owes Charlie $40.
Calculate Net Balances: Alice: -$40, Bob: $0, Charlie: +$40.
Simplify graph: Eliminate intermediary Bob. Alice pays Charlie $40 directly (1 transaction instead of 2).

step_by_step_explanation: 1. Strategy Pattern for Splits: ISplitStrategy isolates validation and percentage/exact calculation math from balance recording.
2. Directed Debt Graph: balanceSheet[A][B] cleanly models pairwise debts where opposite entries cancel out ($A \to B = - B \to A$).
3. Min-Cash-Flow Debt Simplification: Reduces $O(N^2)$ transaction volume down to $O(N)$ transfers by computing net balances and greedily pairing largest debtors with largest creditors.
4. High Numeric Precision: Uses threshold-based floating point comparisons ($< 0.01$) to prevent floating point residual display bugs.

common_mistakes.mistake: Float rounding issues causing 3-way split of $100 to sum to $99.99
common_mistakes.correction: Assign fractional remainder cents to the first participant or store values in integer cents (e.g. 10000 cents).

interview_traps:
Trap: 'How do you prevent money creation/loss due to floating point precision errors?'
Answer: Use 64-bit integer values representing smallest currency units (cents, paise, satoshis) rather than double.

code_refactor_exercise.problem: Refactor an expense calculation where percentage and exact split math are combined in a giant 200-line switch case.
code_refactor_exercise.good_code: Use Strategy Pattern with ISplitStrategy and clean unit tests for each strategy.

practice_problem.title: Design Group Expense Settlement
practice_problem.description: Add a `Group` entity that isolates balance sheets strictly within a vacation trip or shared apartment.
practice_problem.hint: Create `Group` class holding its own `balanceSheet` and `ExpenseHistory` list.

topics.title: Movie Ticket Booking System (Intermediate)
topics.definition: A high-concurrency seat reservation and movie ticketing platform managing multiplex cinema halls, show timings, transient seat locking (10-minute hold), and payment confirmations.
topics.why_it_matters: The standard problem for testing **Distributed/In-Memory Locking**, **State Transitions**, and **Time-to-Live (TTL) seat release** under massive burst traffic.
topics.real_world_analogy: Booking opening-night IMAX tickets for Avengers on BookMyShow: 50,000 users click the same 5 best seats at 12:00:00. Exactly 1 user gets a 10-minute lock; if payment fails, the seat unlocks automatically.
conceptual_breakdown: Core Hierarchy: City $\to$ CinemaHall $\to$ Auditorium / Screen $\to$ Show $\to$ Seat.
Seat Locking State Machine: Available $\to$ Locked (10 min TTL) $\to$ Booked / Released.
Optimistic vs Pessimistic Locking: Guarding concurrent seat reservations across multiple cluster workers.
Payment Confirmation Webhook: Converts temporary lock into permanent Booking record.

steps.description: User 1 selects Seat B5. SeatLockManager acquires mutex, marks B5 LOCKED with 10-minute expiry.
User 2 tries to reserve Seat B5. Request rejected: Seat is currently locked by another user.
User 1 payment fails or times out. SeatLockManager automatically releases B5 back to AVAILABLE.
User 2 retries and successfully locks Seat B5.

step_by_step_explanation: 1. Atomic Multi-Seat Locking: All requested seats are verified and locked under a single critical section, preventing partial reservation deadlocks.
2. Time-To-Live (TTL) Lock Expiry: Lock includes a timestamp expiration; expired locks are automatically treated as available without requiring an active background sweeper thread.
3. Ownership Validation on Payment: Booking confirmation guarantees that only the user holding the active lock can finalize the purchase.

comparison_matrix.title: Concurrency Locking Strategies for Ticketing
rows: High abort rate on hot seats

common_mistakes.mistake: Locking seats one-by-one without sorted ordering leading to deadlocks
common_mistakes.correction: Sort seat IDs before acquiring locks to guarantee global hierarchy acquisition.

common_mistakes.mistake: Permanently locking seats if payment webhook crashes
common_mistakes.correction: Always attach a TTL (Time-To-Live) to every provisional reservation.

interview_traps:
Trap: 'How do you prevent two users simultaneously booking adjacent seats when social distancing rules require 1 empty seat between parties?'
Answer: Encapsulate validation inside a ReservationValidator pipeline that checks adjacent row/col status during the atomic lock step.

code_refactor_exercise.problem: Refactor a seat booking service where database queries and payment processing occur while holding the global mutex.
code_refactor_exercise.good_code: Acquire temporary lock with TTL -> release lock -> process payment asynchronously -> acquire lock briefly to finalize.

practice_problem.title: Design VIP Dynamic Tier Pricing
practice_problem.description: Implement surge pricing that automatically increases remaining seat prices by 20% once occupancy reaches 80%.
practice_problem.hint: Use Strategy pattern for dynamic pricing calculations based on occupancy percentage.

topics.title: Ride Sharing System (Intermediate)
topics.definition: A location-based dynamic dispatch and ride-hailing service managing geospatial driver location updates, nearest-driver matching, surge pricing, and trip lifecycle state.
topics.why_it_matters: Demonstrates geospatial indexing (QuadTree/Geohash), Strategy Pattern for driver matching, and State Pattern for trip lifecycle (Requested, Assigned, Arrived, InTrip, Completed).
topics.real_world_analogy: Requesting an UberX: app converts your GPS coordinates to a Geohash, queries spatial index for idle drivers within 3 km, matches best driver, and begins live trip telemetry.
conceptual_breakdown: Geospatial Driver Index: Grid/QuadTree or Geohash mapping lat/lon coordinates to active driver IDs.
Trip Lifecycle State Machine: REQUESTED $\to$ DRIVER_MATCHED $\to$ IN_PROGRESS $\to$ COMPLETED.
Matching Strategy: IMatchingStrategy (Nearest Driver vs Highest Rated Driver vs Batch Dispatch).
Fare Estimation Strategy: Base fare + time duration + distance + surge multiplier.

steps.description: Rider requests ride from Location A to Location B.
TripManager queries SpatialIndex for nearby available drivers within 5km.
Nearest driver D1 receives match and accepts ride.
Trip status transitions to IN_PROGRESS as driver begins navigation.
Trip completes at destination. Fare calculated and charged.

step_by_step_explanation: 1. Spatial Matching Strategy: IMatchingStrategy decouples proximity algorithms from ride management.
2. Driver Availability Management: Driver state switches atomically between available and in-trip.
3. End-to-End Trip Lifecycle: Clean transition from Requested to Completed with telemetry position updates.

common_mistakes.mistake: Locking the entire driver pool during matching
common_mistakes.correction: Partition spatial index by city geohash cells to isolate locks.

interview_traps:
Trap: 'What happens if a driver rejects a dispatch offer?'
Answer: Introduce an OfferTimeout state machine: if rejected/timed out, mark driver temporarily skipped for this trip and query the strategy for next best driver.

code_refactor_exercise.problem: Refactor a hardcoded driver search loop inside Trip class into a standalone Matching Engine.
code_refactor_exercise.good_code: Isolate matching in IMatchingStrategy with dependency injection.

practice_problem.title: Design Shared / Carpool Rides (UberPool)
practice_problem.description: Extend the ride system to allow 2 riders with overlapping pickup and destination trajectories to share the same vehicle.
practice_problem.hint: Use Route waypoint optimization to calculate detour delta before accepting second passenger.

topics.title: Thread-safe LRU Cache (Advanced)
topics.definition: A high-performance in-memory key-value cache combining $O(1)$ Hash Map lookups with a Doubly Linked List for Least-Recently-Used eviction, protected by fine-grained thread synchronization.
topics.why_it_matters: One of the most frequently asked systems design questions at FAANG. Evaluates low-level data structure manipulation, pointer management, and reader-writer locking.
topics.real_world_analogy: CPU L1/L2 hardware cache lines or in-memory Redis key eviction where oldest unused web pages are dropped when memory limit is reached.
conceptual_breakdown: Doubly Linked List: Maintains access order from Head (Most Recently Used) to Tail (Least Recently Used). $O(1)$ node removal and prepend.
Hash Map: unordered_map provides $O(1)$ key lookup.
Thread Safety: std::shared_mutex allows concurrent multi-threaded readers while exclusive write locks protect list restructuring.
Eviction Flow: When size exceeds capacity, tail node is severed from list and erased from hash map.

interactive_animation.title: LRU Cache Eviction and Lookup Cycle

steps.description: Cache with capacity=2 has elements [A, B].
get('A') is called. Node 'A' is detached and moved to Head.
put('C', val) is called. Capacity full! Tail node 'B' is evicted and erased from Hash Map.
New node 'C' is inserted at Head.

step_by_step_explanation: 1. O(1) Access and Reordering: Hash map provides pointer to Doubly Linked List node in $O(1)$. Pointer manipulation re-links head/tail in $O(1)$.
2. Sentinel-less Node Detachment: Explicit head/tail updates cleanly handle single-element and empty-list edge cases.
3. Mutex Locking Discipline: Because get() modifies node position in the list (making it MRU), a write lock is required even during read operations.

common_mistakes.correction: `get()` modifies linked list pointers to make the accessed item MRU, causing data races if multiple threads run read locks. Use `std::unique_lock` or a striped lock LRU.
Always delete the severed tail node when erasing from hash map.

interview_traps:
Trap: 'Why can't you use std::list and std::unordered_map?'
Answer: While `std::list::splice` is $O(1)$, standard library list nodes have additional heap overhead and cannot be embedded directly into custom memory arenas for ultra-low latency.

code_refactor_exercise.problem: Refactor an LRU cache that uses a single vector and linear element shifting on every lookup.
code_refactor_exercise.bad_code: vector search -> erase element -> push_front (O(N) operations)
code_refactor_exercise.good_code: Use Doubly Linked List + Hash Map for true O(1) amortized performance.

practice_problem.title: Design Sharded / Striped Thread-Safe LRU
practice_problem.description: Build a 16-stripe LRU cache where keys are hashed to independent LRU shards to eliminate thread contention across 64 cores.
practice_problem.hint: Create array of `ThreadSafeLRUCache` shards; pick shard via `std::hash<K>{}(key) % NumShards`.

topics.title: Rate Limiter System (Advanced)
topics.definition: A high-throughput API throttling and traffic-shaping component implementing Token Bucket, Leaky Bucket, and Sliding Window Log algorithms to prevent DDoS and API abuse.
topics.why_it_matters: A critical system component asked in almost every senior backend LLD interview. Evaluates algorithm selection, thread-safety, and time-drift handling.
topics.real_world_analogy: A highway toll booth gate that releases 1 vehicle every 2 seconds regardless of whether 50 cars arrive simultaneously in a burst.
conceptual_breakdown: Token Bucket Algorithm: Tokens added at constant rate up to capacity; requests consume tokens; supports bursts.
Leaky Bucket Algorithm: Requests enter a FIFO queue; drained at constant leak rate; smooths bursts into steady stream.
Sliding Window Counter: Blends previous window count with current window elapsed fraction for accurate burst protection without full log memory overhead.
Client Identification: Throttles per IP, API Key, or User ID.

steps.description: Bucket starts at max capacity = 5 tokens. Refill rate = 1 token/sec.
Burst of 3 requests arrives. 3 tokens consumed. 2 tokens remaining. Requests ALLOWED.
Burst of 3 requests arrives immediately. 2 tokens consumed, 1 request REJECTED (429 Too Many Requests).
2 seconds pass. 2 new tokens refilled. New request arrives and is ALLOWED.

step_by_step_explanation: 1. Lazy Token Refill: Rather than running background timer threads for every client, tokens are lazily refilled on-demand during the request.
2. Monotonic Clock Usage: Uses std::chrono::steady_clock to prevent system clock adjustments (NTP sync) from corrupting token math.
3. Burst Friendly: Allows short burst up to maxCapacity while enforcing steady-state average rate.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using `std::chrono::system_clock` which can drift or jump backwards on NTP sync
Spawning a background thread per client to tick tokens
common_mistakes.correction: Use lazy mathematical evaluation based on elapsed delta-time.

interview_traps:
Trap: 'How do you handle rate limiting across 100 distributed load balancer nodes?'
Answer: Use Redis Lua scripts implementing token bucket or Sliding Window Counter to make atomicity global across all API gateways.

code_refactor_exercise.problem: Refactor a fixed window rate limiter that suffers from the 2x burst traffic spike at the minute boundary.
code_refactor_exercise.bad_code: if (currentMinute == lastMinute) { count++; if (count > limit) drop(); }
code_refactor_exercise.good_code: Implement Token Bucket or Sliding Window Log.

practice_problem.title: Design Sliding Window Counter Limiter
practice_problem.description: Implement the Cloudflare sliding window counter algorithm that weights current window vs previous window counts.

topics.title: Pub/Sub In-Memory Message Queue (Advanced)
topics.definition: A thread-safe in-memory publish-subscribe broker supporting multiple topics, concurrent consumer groups, message offset tracking, and asynchronous dispatch.
topics.why_it_matters: Core architecture behind Apache Kafka and RabbitMQ. Tests concurrency, Producer-Consumer synchronization with condition variables, and Observer pattern at scale.
topics.real_world_analogy: A radio broadcasting network: radio stations (Publishers) broadcast music to named frequencies (Topics), and individual cars (Subscribers) tune into frequencies and play music independently.
conceptual_breakdown: Topic & Partition: An ordered, append-only log of Message items.
Producer: Publishes messages to designated topics.
Consumer Group & Offsets: Each consumer maintains its own integer offset index into the topic message log.
Broker Engine: Manages topic creation, thread-safe message appending, and condition variable wakeups.

steps.description: Producer publishes Message M1 to Topic 'orders'. Message appended at Offset 0.
Consumer Group A (Analytics) reads Offset 0 and processes M1.
Consumer Group B (Billing) reads Offset 0 independently at its own pace.
Producer appends M2 at Offset 1. Consumers notified via condition variable.

step_by_step_explanation: 1. Append-Only Topic Log: Messages are immutable records with monotonically increasing integer offsets.
2. Consumer Offset Independence: Each consumer tracks its own read position, allowing different services to replay or lag safely.
3. Efficient Condition Variable Signaling: Consumers sleep without spinning CPU until new messages are appended.

common_mistakes.mistake: Erasing messages when first consumer reads them
common_mistakes.correction: Retain topic log so multiple independent consumer groups can read the same stream.

interview_traps:
Trap: 'How do you guarantee exactly-once message delivery in C++ LLD?'
Answer: Pair idempotent consumer processing with transactional outbox or deduplication hash sets tracking processed message UUIDs.

code_refactor_exercise.problem: Refactor a point-to-point single-consumer queue into a multi-subscriber broadcast topic.
code_refactor_exercise.good_code: vector log with offset tracking per subscriber

practice_problem.title: Design Partitioned Topic with Key Hashing
practice_problem.description: Extend Topic to support 4 partitions where messages with the same `partitionKey` are strictly guaranteed FIFO ordering.
practice_problem.hint: Route messages to partition index via `std::hash<string>{}(key) % numPartitions`.

topics.title: Stock Trading Matching Order Book (Advanced)
topics.definition: An ultra-low-latency financial matching engine organizing Buy (Bids) and Sell (Asks) orders by Price-Time Priority and executing trades at matching price points.
topics.why_it_matters: The highest-tier LLD problem for fintech and quantitative trading firms (Citadel, Jane Street, Optiver, Goldman Sachs). Evaluates cache-friendly data structures, zero-allocation algorithms, and priority matching.
topics.real_world_analogy: NASDAQ or NYSE limit order book: traders submit 'Buy 100 AAPL @ $150' and 'Sell 50 AAPL @ $150'; the matching engine instantly matches 50 shares at $150 and keeps the remaining 50 Buy limit order open.
conceptual_breakdown: Order Entity: id, side (BUY/SELL), price, quantity, timestamp.
Limit Level: A FIFO queue (doubly linked list) of orders at the exact same price.
Price Ladder (Bids & Asks): Bids sorted in descending order (highest price first); Asks sorted in ascending order (lowest price first).
Price-Time Priority Matching: Best price matches first; if prices match, oldest order matches first.

steps.description: Order Book Bids: [100 shares @ $150]. Asks: [50 shares @ $152].
Incoming Market Buy Order: 50 shares. Crosses book against best Ask ($152).
Trade Executed: 50 shares @ $152. Ask level $152 is completely filled and removed.

step_by_step_explanation: 1. Price-Time Priority Ladder: std::map maintains sorted price levels while std::deque enforces strict FIFO matching for equal prices.
2. Crossing Book Execution: Trade prices default to the resting maker order's price point.
3. Efficient Level Pruning: Empty price levels are erased immediately to keep tree searches fast.

common_mistakes.correction: Represent prices as integer cents (e.g. 15000 cents for $150.00) to eliminate IEEE 754 precision drift.

interview_traps:
Trap: 'How do high-frequency trading (HFT) engines cancel orders in O(1) time without iterating the deque?'
Answer: Use an intrusive doubly-linked list for each limit level combined with an `unordered_map` lookup map.

code_refactor_exercise.problem: Refactor an order book where double floating point prices cause orders at $10.00000001 not to match $10.00.
code_refactor_exercise.good_code: using Price = int64_t; // in fixed precision micro-units

practice_problem.title: Design O(1) Order Cancellation
practice_problem.description: Implement an intrusive Doubly Linked List Order node so `cancelOrder(uint64_t orderId)` executes in strictly O(1) time.
practice_problem.hint: Store node pointers in a hash table `unordered_map<uint64_t, Order*>`.
